all_of: attacker-supplied CSS is served same-origin and loaded into a page only an admin bot can see
the secret the bot's page carries is TEXT CONTENT, not an attribute, so attribute-selector exfiltration does not apply
the CSP leaves exactly one host-wildcarded directive, here font-src 'self' *, which is the whole exfiltration channel
the secret's alphabet is known and its generator SORTS it, so the SET of characters determines the string
the privileged endpoint trusts a connection-derived value (req.ip == 127.0.0.1) rather than a credential, so the bot's own fetch satisfies it
a later endpoint interpolates a request value into a SQLite LIMIT clause
any_of: the admin page keeps the secret in an element hidden with a utility class, which attacker CSS can simply re-show
the bot dwells on the page long enough for font loads to complete

chain.action: read the token generator before touching the page: TokenHelper shuffles a 62-character dictionary, takes 32, and then sorts them
chain.why: this is what makes the whole chain cheap. A sorted string is fully determined by its character SET, and a set is exactly what a unicode-range leak returns. Without this the same leak would only narrow the search

chain.action: read the CSP as a list of what is NOT allowed: default-src 'self', img-src 'self', style-src 'self', object-src 'none', and font-src 'self' *
chain.why: one directive carries a host wildcard and it is the only way out. Background-image exfiltration is dead under img-src 'self', so the leak has to be a font load

chain.action: submit CSS with one @font-face per alphabet character, all sharing one font-family, each with its own unicode-range and its own URL; apply that family to the secret's element and override the utility class that hides it with display:block !important
chain.why: the browser downloads a face only when a character inside its unicode-range is actually rendered, so the set of URLs that get requested IS the set of characters in the secret. The element must be visible for anything to be rendered at all, and the hiding class uses !important so the override needs it too

chain.action: sort the leaked characters to recover the token, then submit a second stylesheet whose @font-face src is the same-origin privileged URL with that token in it, applied to an element that renders
chain.why: the privileged route is gated on the request's source address, not on a session, so it cannot be called from outside. The bot's own browser is inside, and a font load is a GET the bot performs; font-src includes 'self', so the CSP permits it. This is the step that needs no external host at all

chain.action: with the submission now approved, post one comment and then blind-extract through the LIMIT clause: LIMIT (SELECT CASE WHEN <predicate> THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) returns one row or none
chain.why: SQLite accepts any scalar expression as LIMIT, so row count becomes a one-bit oracle. Binary-search unicode(substr(...)) per position to read sqlite_master for the randomised table name and then the flag out of it

first_confirming_probe.request: submit a stylesheet containing a single @font-face with an absolute URL on a host you control and font-family applied to body, then wait for the bot
first_confirming_probe.expected: one request arrives at your listener: the bot loads attacker CSS and font-src really does permit an external host
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: nothing arrives. Before blaming the challenge, check the two failure modes in the traps: a tunnel that intercepts browser user agents, and a stylesheet URL that 404s because the file is written asynchronously after the bot is dispatched

blast_radius: Read-only against the target apart from rows it is designed to accept: a few submissions, one comment, and one submission flipped to approved. None of those can be removed without the reject token, so keep the count low. The real exposure is on YOUR side: this chain needs a public listener, so a tunnel is opened to the internet for the duration. Bind the listener to loopback, keep the tunnel up only for the leak, and tear it down and verify it is refusing connections afterwards. Nothing but font paths ever reaches it.

verification.evidence: Live HTB instance. The unicode-range stylesheet produced exactly 32 font requests out of 62 offered, whose sorted characters gave the token; a second stylesheet pointing a font at the same-origin approve route flipped /view/4 from 403 to 200; the LIMIT oracle then yielded the table name flag_dd38f088 and the flag. Recorded in challenges/stylish/state.json through tools/hooks.py post-probe (confirms, evidence-kind class then impact) and pre-flag (source live-response). Tunnel and listener were torn down afterwards and verified refusing.

reuse_when: attacker-controlled CSS reaches a page that someone more privileged renders, and the CSP still leaves one directive with a host wildcard: read the CSP as the list of channels the author forgot to close
a secret is text content rather than an attribute, which rules out the usual [attr^=...] selector leak: reach for @font-face plus unicode-range, which leaks the character set
the character set alone is enough whenever the secret's generator sorts, dedupes, or otherwise fixes the order; always read the generator before assuming a leak is only partial

a privileged route trusts req.ip, X-Forwarded-For or any other connection-derived value instead of a credential: stop trying to call it and find something already inside that can be made to fetch a URL
a headless bot is that something: any CSS-reachable URL is a GET performed from inside, and font-src 'self' makes same-origin ones legal
a request value lands in a SQLite LIMIT: LIMIT takes an arbitrary scalar expression, so row count is a free boolean oracle even with no error output and no UNION
known_traps: ngrok's free tier is unusable as the listener here. Its browser interstitial fires on the bot's Chrome user agent, answers 200 with its own HTML, and the request never reaches your server; a curl test passes and hides the problem. Measured: same URL, curl reaches the listener, browser user agent does not. ngrok TCP endpoints would avoid it but are card-gated on a free account (ERR_NGROK_8013). An ssh reverse tunnel (localhost.run) passed browser user agents straight through.

guard against JavaScript truthiness in the oracle: the route checks `if (submissionID && pagination)` and a numeric 0 is falsy, so it falls through and sends NO response at all. That reads as a client timeout rather than an answer. Send pagination as a STRING so "0" stays truthy and still means LIMIT 0.

the stylesheet is written with an asynchronous fs.writeFile and the bot is dispatched on the same tick, so the first visit can race the file into existence. Confirm the file is actually served at /card_styles/<id>.css before concluding the CSS is not being applied.

the secret's element is hidden by a utility class that uses !important, so display:block alone does nothing and no character is ever rendered. The override needs !important too, and if the element is not rendered no font is ever requested, which looks exactly like the leak failing.

only the element you style leaks. The page carries a second token in an identically hidden element; leaving it hidden keeps its characters out of the result, which is what makes the 32 hits unambiguous rather than a union of two tokens.
the flag table name is randomised per boot, so read sqlite_master first; PRAGMA case_sensitive_like=ON is set, so a LIKE pattern has to match the real case.

a stale module-shadowing file in the working directory will break the extractor before it sends a single request (a local inspect.py shadowed the standard library here). Keep exploit scripts out of directories holding files named after standard modules.
